subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT TO BE PRESENTED ON MONDAY, JUNE 1
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are
proceeded with, I should like to intimate to the house that for two reasons I shall not be able to proceed with the budget until Monday next. On Monday afternoon, with the consent of the house, I propose to proceed with it. Perhaps, strictly speaking, consent is not required, for the motion is that the house resolve itself into committee of ways and means, and not into committee of supply. I
Alberta Coal

propose :to present the budget on Monday afternoon, and I shall leave to my right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) the determination as to when the debate shall be resumed, whether on the succeeding Thursday or on Tuesday; or whatever other day he may select will be satisfactory under the circumstances. I had previously told this house that I thought we should be able to present the budget before the last day of May. The last day of May falls on Sunday, and I shall not be able to present the budget in May for two reasons, one of which I have already mentioned to the house. There has also been delay in receiving a cable affecting certain matters concerning one of the overseas dominions. The other reason is the physical work of completing certain of the matters that have to be dealt with. I trust, therefore, that the house will not regard the presentation of the budget on Monday as being in any sense a breach of my undertaking to endeavour to present it before the last day of May, That day falling on Sunday, I shall present the budget on Monday.

speechtext:

Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) deals with the farms at Indian Head and Sutherland which are supplying free nursery stock to the farmers of the west. The first of these stations was established at Indian Head twenty-five years ago, and later one was established at Sutherland. Both are in the province of Saskatchewan, and as I said, the purpose of these stations is to supply free nursery stock to the farmers of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Oh no. If my hon. friend will give me a moment I will come to that. The provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta assumed administration of their natural resources on October 1, 1930, and as no provision had been made in the transfer agreement covering the matter, the Department of the Interior, through the forestry branch, has continued to administer those stations. The stations were supplying a service only to the three western provinces, and it might well be argued that if that service did not apply to the other provinces of Canada the stations became a matter of provincial re-

The committee will
resume consideration of the following item:
Dairying, including grant of $5,000 to National Dairy Council, $295,000.
And the amendment thereto of Mr. Young.-

Mr. Chairman, before we
continue discussion of the various items in this department, I wish to refer to a matter, which was brought up the other evening, of vital importance to the department and to the officials of the department. The matter to which I refer, which deeply concerns the people of Canada as a whole and particularly of western Canada, has reference to a statement which was read into Hansard by the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance). He read from a report which appeared in a newspaper of western Canada. To recall the article to the minds of hon. members I shall read it again.
There has never been a department ' in Ottawa so incompetent, in such a state of inefficiency and disorganization as agriculture when W. R. Motherwell left it. The department was and still is inefficiently manned, permeated with intrigue, jealousies and incompetence. Mr. Motherwell gave no thought to agriculture.
Later on in the article are these words:
It was under these conditions that Mr. Weir took office. He had scarcely a competent official, and many were disloyal to him. He did not tell the whole story last night, but 9n his estimates parliament will receive further information on the decrepit department left by Mr. Motherwell.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that article constitutes a reflection on the officials of the Department of Agriculture which should not be allowed to pass without comment. The other night the minister made no comment on the statement. So far as the ex-Minister of Agriculture is concerned we will leave his administration to the judgment of the people of the country, and especially to those of western Canada.
You did.
They have always been of the opinion that the Hon. Mr. Motherwell was one of the best Ministers of Agriculture this country ever had. The farmers of western Canada-

What did they say on July 28?



Supply-Agriculture-Dairying

I can wait as 'long as my hon. friend. The fanners of western Canada vealize that Mr. Motherwell, the ex-minister [DOT]of Agriculture, did more for agriculture in western Canada and in Canada as a whole than any other person in this country. I am concerned with the statement that the Department of Agriculture is incompetent, and that the officials are inefficient. If that is the case I say we should not vote a single item [DOT] in these estimates for the department until the condition is corrected. I ask the minister to-day if he is in agreement with the statement that the officials in the department are incompetent and inefficient. If so the people of Canada should know; if the statement is not true they should know that the officials are competent and efficient. I think a statement should be made in fairness not only to the people of Canada but to the officials of the department who are resting under this sort of suspicion.

Mr. Chairman, the other night
when the article referred to was read into Hansard I did not make a statement because I did not think it was worth while. I do not know who the editor of the paper is or who prompted the article. When speaking on the public platform and in the house, since taking the portfolio of Agriculture, I have on every occasion spoken in the kindest terms of my predecessor and will always think of him in the kindest possible way. So far as the officials of the department are concerned I do not think the article requires an answer. I believe my action since taking over the department supplies the best answer possible. Although we have in the neighbourhood of 2,500 officials on the staff I doubt if ever on the occasion of a change in the head of a department, fewer dismissals have taken place than since I became Minister of Agriculture. *With the exception of two or three I know of no dismissals in the department.
The minister has said he has made practically no dismissals. The article to which I have referred has been appearing in newspapers throughout western Canada.
The minister is not responsible for that.

I think this is a matter which should be properly cleared up. If there are any incompetent or inefficient officials I would say they should be dismissed. They should not be allowed to carry on the important work of a department of government.
[Mr. Hanson.1
The hon. member need not worry about that; he is in the opposition.
Of course I am in the opposition, and I would say the same thing if I were on the government side of the house.

The hon. member would
not have opened his mouth.

Hon. gentlemen opposite
seem to think that because we happen to be on the opposition side we are not concerned with the government of the country. It is the duty of the opposition carefully to watch the expenditures made and the work done on behalf of the Canadian people. This is a very serious matter. I believe some of the articles which appeared in western newspapers were signed by a reporter who is high in the confidence of the Conservative party. Not only the Department of Agriculture but the whole government is under suspicion if the matter is not properly dealt with. I think the Minister of Agriculture should concern himself a little more about this item than he has done. He has simply been telling us that there were no dismissals. Sometimes incompetent and inefficient officials are allowed to stay in the department, perhaps not discovered, and I think the minister should give a little better explanation of this item.

Mr. Chairman, I have
listened with some interest to the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Totzke), but I think he had better start to criticize the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan), who has been parading around the country running down the Minister of Agriculture before that hon. gentleman has hardly taken his seat. I have before me a newspaper clipping of a statement made by the hon. member, which, I think, is very far-fetched and not at all fair to the -Minister. This is the clipping:
Mr. McMillan criticized the agricultural policy of the Conservative federal government as inadequate and unavailing. The government, he said, had gone "protectionist crazy."
Hear, hear.

Well. I can only say that when you gentlemen opposite picked up the Dunning budget I don't know how crazy you were, but I think you were crazier than we were. Let me complete the quotation:
He cited facts to show that dairymen and also fruit and vegetable growers in Canada had suffered through the tariff policy of the Conservatives.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
The hon. member should know better than that. I always thought he was pretty fair to the cattle industry and to farming in general, but he certainly is not fair in the statements I have quoted, which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of May 18, 1931.
Now, I wonder if some hon. members on the other side can intelligently discuss this important item before the committee? Do you know it is said throughout the constituency that I have the honour to represent that no commercial traveller will get off at railway stations in ridings represented by some members opposite who just talk wheat, and wheat alone.
Oh, oh.

No, they will not get
off at those stations to sell goods unless they see cream cans on the platform. I am proud to tell the committee that at every station platform throughout the constituency of Marquette they do get off and are prepared to sell goods; you can see cream cans on every station platform in my constituency. True, I admit prices have gone down. But why? Would any body of men make such a fool treaty as you made with Australia? Would you do it again if you had the chance and provide us the material that we had to go to the country with at the last election? No, I do not think you would; I think you would know a little more about the cow; and you had better get acquainted with her, you had better get to know more about her. She was the first pioneer that came to Canada. She came here with Champlain, and she has stayed with us right along. You are upholding the late Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). I have nothing to say against him personally. His constituency and mine adjoin each other, and I have known him a great many years. But although I am not going to say anything about him personally, I will say this of his policy:	I venture to
assert that the present Minister of Agriculture will never involve the country in an expense of about $9,500,000 sending professors chasing through the country to find out whether moths' eggs are fertile or unfertile; nor will he have them chasing around the country, as I have seen them in western Canada, to find out whether rye or barley has whiskers. Certainly the present minister will not do that and ignore the cattle business. Was there anything so ridiculous as that iniquitous transaction of the Petersen commission that the former minister was responsible for? And what was the result of it? It cost the country $35,000. What did it get for us? It got us nothing. Any time our friends 22110-130t
opposite touch the cattle business they seem to make a mess of it. They have never had a constructive policy in regard to live stock. What did the hon. member opposite do while he was Minister of Agriculture? He discontinued the policy of distributing pure-bred sires throughout the country. That was the worst course he could have taken at the very time that the Irish government had their representatives here looking over the country to see what we were doing. They at once realized our mistake and on their return to Ireland they adopted our former policy and captured the British market. Look at the position we are in today owing to the lack of attention of our friends opposite to the dairy industry. This item before the committee is a very important one and concerns the dairy industry. Oh, yes, the cow is our friend. As I stated during our campaign, some of you gentlemen opposite don't know where milk comes from; you think it comes from a bottle.
Oh, oh.

Yes. I wonder if you
know what a cow is? I have a clipping here and I will read it for the benefit of some hon. members opposite:
The cow is a female-
Oh, oh.

I have been asked foolish questions by some of those professional men on the opposite side, and therefore I want to read this article for their benefit. I asked one hon. gentleman opposite a certain question in reference to a cow, and he looked at me with anmzement and could not answer- he could not tell me which end of her got up first. So I am going to tell you what a cow is. This is an excellent article written by a student in a Minnesota college. I thought it was only right that some members here should know something about the cow so they would not ask such foolish questions about her. Let me proceed.
The cow is a female quadruped with an alto voice and a countenance in which there is no guile. She collaborates with the pump in the production of a liquid called milk, provides the filler for hash, sausages and similar objects, and at last is skinned by those she has benefited, as mortals commonly are.
The young cow is called a calf, and is used in the manufacture of chicken salad, breaded veal and other uses of which no further knowledge is necessary.
The cow's tail-
I want you to know where it is mounted.
The cow's tail is mounted aft and has a universal joint. It is used to disturb maraud-
204S

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
ing flies and the tassel on the end has unique educational value. Persons who come in contact with the tassel have vocabularies of peculiar and impressive force.
The cow has two stomachs.
One of my hon. friends opposite did not know that she had two stomachs.
The one on the ground floor is used as a warehouse and has no other function. When this one is filled,, the cow retires to a quiet spot where her bad manners will occasion no comment. The raw material thus conveyed for the second time to the interior of her face is pulverized and delivered to the auxiliary stomach, where it is converted into cow.
The cow has no upper plate.
Now, get that. I was asked by an hon. gentleman:	"How many teeth has she in her
upper jaw?" I said to him, "Don't you know? Have you ever looked a cow over on the farm?" He said, "No; I looked over the fence at a cow and that is as near as I ever got to seeing her teeth."
The cow has no upper plate. All of her teeth are parked in the lower part of her face. This arrangement was perfected by an efficiency expert to keep her from gumming things up. As a result she bites up and gums down.
If we paid more attention to the cow, the mother of prosperity, Canada would be in a unique position to-day. I may tell you I have spent fifty years of my life among the cattle of western Canada, and I make no apology when I use these words on the floor of the house. I may tell you, sir, for your information that the cow played an important part in the last election; she went a long way to defeat hon. members opposite. Discontinuing the policy of putting out pure-bred sires was suicide to the cattle industry of western Canada. I wonder why hon. gentlemen opposite did a thing like that? When I was putting that to an audience in Angusville, Manitoba, one good cow within hearing bellowed out and seemed to say, "You are absolutely correct."
The question before the committee is one of vital importance to our western country. We want to get back into the dairy industry, and we want to get back to raising good dual purpose calves. We want the right type of calves, and we want no obstruction to items such as the one before the house at the present time. Why do hon. members obstruct an item of this kind? Whenever it has been a question of live stock hon. gentlemen opposite have been obstructionists; they have put the industry in the position in which it is in to-day. We had no business to lose that trade with England. We have Ireland shipping

a million cattle a year, while Canada shipped none during 1926, 1927 and 1928. We lost that trade entirely when we should have been building it up.
Will the hon. member tell us exactly why we were not able to ship cattle during that period, and why Ireland did ship cattle?

Ask me
another.

I will ask you a question in a moment. Will the hon. member for Marquette, who knows a great deal about the cattle industry, tell us why Canada did not ship cattle while Ireland was shipping cattle? At the same time he might answer this question: Can he tell me any great agricultural country that ever followed the policy hon. gentlemen opposite are attempting to put across now?
I cannot hear my hon. friend very plainly, so I cannot answer.
It was not intelligent anyway.

If the section of the
country represented by my hon. friend had taken up the production of breeding live stock it would not be in the position it is to-day. When hon. gentlemen opposite took office we were shipping 220,000,000 pounds of bacon annually to England, while now we are shipping only 20,000,000 pounds and a few straggling cattle. We should be shipping cattle daily by the thousands from Montreal. They would be bringing back real money, and I trust that hon. members will look fairly at these items being brought forward by the minister, and will not throw any barriers in the way of their passing.

We all like to have a little fun with the hon. member for Marquette, but that will scarcely answer the question asked by the hon. member for Humboldt. I want to assure the house I did not know the hon. member was going to raise that question to-day.
He said you were single.

My hon. friend
might be so good as to keep quiet just now. I did not like to bring up the question when the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) raised it the other night; it looked so horrible and terrible that I hesitated to say anything about it. My hon. friend the minister has given a qualified denial. I

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
wonder if she could speak also on behalf of his chief secretary and say there are no reports coming from that source, because I continually hear, not only in Ottawa but in Regina and other places, every time the minister goes west, a bunch of rumours regarding the terrible condition in which he found the Department of Agriculture.
I know pretty well who wrote this particular article; I do not know whether or not he is in the gallery just now. Having regard to the fact that there is a wonderful similarity between that article and the article which the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) denied, in which he was included among those making cowardly attacks upon the minister, I assume this article is by the same author, and lest my silence be interpreted as assent with reference to departmental officials, I think it my duty to say a word with regard to the matter.
I am not going to say anything concerning the references to myself; I do not think I have to do that, but I believe I should defend the officials of the department, no matter who is the slanderer. I do not know where in this country you will find a better lot of men. I had the good fortune to have an excellent staff in Regina, a staff largely of my own selection. I accepted the staff which was here at the time I took office, and as far as I can recall only one new branch was established here in the nine years I had charge of the department. Some of the officials have been here for thirty years, under five or six ministers, and for that reason I feel greater freedom to speak on their behalf than perhaps would be the case if I had been given the opportunity of selecting them myself.
The administrative head of any department of government is the deputy minister. We have the deputy minister of agriculture here to-day, and I often wondered during the years I was at the head of that department what I would do to find a substitute if anything should happen to him. I want to say a substitute could not be found in Canada, in my estimation. I have had a good deal of experience in looking for deputy ministers of agriculture in my own province, and this is one of the most difficult positions to fill. You must have not only a theoretical man but a practical man as well; he must be acceptable to the public, and a good administrator. In the present deputy minister of agriculture we have a further, most invaluable qualification; that of being bilingual, which is something almost indispensable in this country. There is not one branch of agriculture I
know of which he is not familiar, and I have never had a word of disagreement with him. There is a hint in this article of some disaffection and all sorts of intrigue; that is absolutely false. I do not care who said it, it is as false as anything possibly could be.
I could go over all the heads of branches and divisions and make almost the same comment regarding them. Let me take the next one who comes to my mind; I refer to Doctor Archibald. Where would you get a better director of experimental farms in all Canada? Two or three years ago the Russian government made a very attractive offer to him to go to that country and put agriculture on its feet, but notwithstanding the size of the offer he was so much taken up with his present work that he remained with us. Then there is George Clark, the seed commissioner. I can scarcely remember when there was a department of agriculture without George Clark, another exceedingly capable man. There was Mr. Arkell, who recently left the department. I have no reason to think he was asked to leave or anything of the kind; I knew he was thinking of going to some commercial cooperative organization where he felt he had a greater opportunity. He was another first class man.
So it is all along the line with these men. There is Doctor Ruddick, who is looked upon as the dean of the dairy industry in Canada. I can scarcely remember when Doctor Ruddick was not dairy commissioner. He had the opportunity of going to New Zealand to put the cheese and butter industry of that country on its feet; he was asked to organize and establish that industry. He has been here as long as I can remember. He is a thoroughly reliable officer, and if my good friend the minister well keep pretty close to these officers and consult with them, he will not go very far wrong. The recommendations, manifestos and policies which have been enunciated by him from time to time have been referred to already. I do not think they would have been issued had my hon. friend consulted with his officers. He has always intimated since he was appointed that he would be willing to receive recommendations from anyone, but apparently I have not been very fortunate in the ones I offered; they were not received very favourably, but we shall not discuss that any further.
I would like to get back to a discussion of the dairying question, but I do not want to shut off discussion on this item. Some of the matters taken up the other night have been left more or less in the air. In reading

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
over Hansard I notice that the hon. member for South Hastings (Mr. Tummon) suggested that the figures with regard to the production of milk had been cooked by the department. I did not catch at the time what he said, as he mumbled something and then hiked into the corridor.

I made the Statement
that the figures were changed in the year 1929 just previous to the elections and I am prepared to substantiate that statement.

I prefer to take
the official figures issued by Doctor Ruddick based upon the figures of the bureau of statistics.

I can give figures which
are just as accurate as those given 'by the hon. gentleman.

It may be all right to talk, but we cannot accept the talk of my hon. friend or any other hon. member in preference to the official figures which I recited the other evening. I do not know anything about my hon. friend's veracity, I assume it is all right but he will have some trouble proving what he has said. If it is within my power, I will give him an opportunity to do so.

Mr. Chairman, since the
question of the production of milk in Canada was raised the other night, and is now before the committee, I think it is no more than right that I should state the position ivhich I took. When the hon. gentleman vas speaking the other evening he made reference to the milk production of Canada. He gave the following round figures:
Year	Pounds
1925		 12,000,000,000
1926		 13.000,000,000
1927		 14,000,000,000
1928		 14,000,000,000
1929		 14,000,000,000
He mentioned that during the last two years there had been a slight reduction in the production. The government reports show the following production in round figures:
Year	Pounds
1924		 12.000,000.000
1925		 12,600,000,000
1926		 13,407,000,000
1927		 13,060,000,000
In other words, there was a reduction as between 1926 and 1927 amounting to 347,000,000 pounds. These figures are taken from the government reports.
Which ones?

The monthly bulletin
as issued by the bureau of statistics.

I would like my
hon. friend to find them for us.

I can produce them if it is necessary. The reduction in the total production of milk, which is after all the basis of the whole dairying industry, from 1926 to 1927 amounted to 347,000,000 pounds. If that amount of milk, had been converted into butter at the regular ratio it would have amounted to over 14,000,000 pounds, and the strange thing is that we imported that year from the antipodes over 14,000,000 pounds of butter. I have not the figures before me for 1928, but in that year there was another decrease in the ' production of milk. What happened in 1929 just prior to the elections?
What elections?

In 1929, a year before the last federal election a new method of reckoning the production of milk was instituted. It was said that in the three prairie provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan the cows were producing 211 per cent more milk than they had a few years ago, and an increase of 10 per cent had taken place in the rest of the Dominion. Thus the figures for the production of milk were adjusted on that basis and showed the production for 1928, as given by the hon. gentleman. Not only that, but they went back and adjusted the figures for the years 1927, 1926, and even 1925 when the Australian treaty and the New Zealand order in council were passed.
In 1928 and 1929 there were 100,000 less milch cows in the Dominion of Canada than there had been in the years 1925 and 1926. In figuring on the new basis, it was decided that the total production of milk was over 14,000,000,000 pounds. In 1926 there were 3,332,479 milch cows in Canada-I do not mean dairy cattle, but just milch cows-an increase from 1925 of 167,000. The year 1926 is conceded to be the best we have had in the dairying industry. Two years after the Australian treaty and the New Zealand order in council came into effect there was a decrease in the number of milch cows in Canada amounting to 75,215, and there was a further decrease in 1928. Under this new method of reckoning, it is said that the production of milk in Canada in 1928 was 14,512,897,961 pounds, but the only correct reports which the department has in regard to this production are the reports received annually from the cheese factories, the butter factories, the combined butter and cheese factories and

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
condensed milk factories. Each year a report is received from these factories giving the number of pounds of milk received by them and from how many cows received. According to these reports, we find that in 1928, the product of 2,197,237 cows was being used in these factories. In other words, the product of two-thirds of the producing cows m Canada was being sent to these factories, the total amount of milk received was less than seven billion pounds, leaving one-third of the total of milch cows in the Dominion to supply seven or eight billion pounds in order to make up the figures given by the hon. gentleman. In other words, the cows of which the department has no record-one-third of the total milch cows in Canada- had to produce two and one-half times as much as the cows of which they had a record. That is the position in regard to the matter.
We would like to know my hon. friend's authority for all this.

My hon. friend will get the authority if he will go and figure it out, it is all taken from the reports.
The other day it was said that the Conservative party promised the farmers that if they came into power, the farmers would get fifty, sixty or seventy cents a pound for butter. I think I was as active in regard to this question as any hon. member on this side of the house, and I never made any such statement in any speech I made in the house or on any platform during the campaign or before it. What the Conservative party did say was that the dairy farmers of the Dominion of Canada were entitled to their own home market, and that if the Conservatives came into power endeavours would be made to give the dairy farmers their own home market.
They do not have it to-day.
If they do not have it to-day, it is because of what they found on their door-step, left by the previous government.

I do not wish to discourage my hon. friend, but I have under my hand an authentic statement from the dairy commissioner. Last night I stated that the reason I took his figures instead of those from the bureau of statistics was because the dairy commissioner's figures were more complete. My hon. friend goes on making assertions without any particular foundation regarding certain matters.
Oh, oh.
My hon. friends are putting up a barrage under which to hide from the facts of the case.
We are not worrying about my hon. friend for a minute.

My hon. friends
during the election campaign last year made statements which they cannot substantiate. These figures that have been given to me contradict them completely, and yet they have to blather a lot about things that have nothing to do with the case.
If my hon. friend did not like the New Zealand treaty, why did he not cancel it?
We shall have an opportunity of discussing the New Zealand treaty when my hon. friends bring it down.
Mr. Dunning gave notice of cancellation of it.

I wonder who is
doing the blocking now. This is the statement from the dairy commissioner:
Agreeably to your telephone request this morning I beg to hand you herewith statement of estimated volume of milk produced in Canada in the years 1922 to 1929.
It is only an estimate.

It is like any other statement of the sort; it is an estimate. The estimates which we have before us are estimates. It is as authentic as can be secured in view of all the circumstances.
Year	Pounds
1922		9,000,000,000
In order to make it fairer to my hon. friends the other night I put it at 10,000,000,000 pounds, to cover any possible mistake, but now I am going to take it as being 9,000,000,000! pounds.
Year	Pounds
1923		11,000,000,000
1924		12,000,000,000
1925		12,000,000.000
1926		13,000,000,000
1927		14,000.000.000
1928		14,000.000,000
1929		14,000,000,000
ou will understand, of	course, that there
is a large element of estimation in these figures.. We know definitely the quantity of milk which is used in manufactured products such as butter, cheese, condensed milk, milk powder, and the quantity which was exported to the United States but for actual quantity of milk and cream consumed or used in the manufacture of dairy butter, we have no actual data. These figures are based on the calculatiohs made by the bureau of statistics.
With regard to dairy butter we get an estimate from the dairy branch.
Supply-Agriculture-Dairying

There is no way of
finding out.

This is the best
that can be gathered, either by the bureau of statistics or by the dairy branch.

These are reports that
come in from cheese factories, butter factories and combined butter and cheese factories.

I know it is hard for my hon. friends to listen to this. We know they told the people the very opposite and they stand convicted by the figures that I have given. These figures are based on calculations made by the bureau of statistics. I have the bureau of statistics figures in my office, but they are not quite complete. It would be strange if someone had not gone down to the bureau of statistics since the other night in order to find out what figures they have. The figures which I have given are more complete than those of the bureau of statistics.
Election figures.

My hon. friends
have not a leg to stand on. Neither the minister nor his deputy will take a different attitude from that which I am taking, because the minister knows the figures I am giving and he gets his from the same source. My hon. friend across the floor concocted something of a fictitious nature in order to try to get out of a difficult situation.

I object. I said that the figures I read to the house were figures which I could produce from monthly bulletins of the dominion bureau of statistics in regard to agricultural statistics. I am prepared to produce them.

All this talk about figures! There has always been a certain discrepancy between the two lines of statistics. The reason is that the figures of the bureau of statistics are based upon the decennial census and those of. the Department of Agriculture are based upon the quinquennial census; or it may be the other way about; I have forgotten which. But there was no such condition of affairs as described by my hon. friend, as fixing up any figures to suit the occasion. That is an absolute falsehood, I do not care who says it, and I want that to be understood without any reservation whatever.

Did the taking of the
census of Saskatchewan increase the volume of milk that was increased per head of cows?
FMr. Motherwell.]

I am not going to be dragged into a discussion along that line; I am discussing other things just now. Let my hon. friends produce the figures from the bureau of statistics. I could not get from the bureau as complete a report as this. I may be able to produce the statement from the bureau later on.
I have another question in regard to the matter. The other night I asked the minister about the prices of butter at the present time and any other date when the price was as low as it is to-day. The minister might also inform me now if he has any better figures regarding the total production of milk during the years I have mentioned. Do my figures correspond or conflict with his?

There is another thought which came to my mind a moment ago, which bears directly on the subject before us. This committee has been little bilt more than a bull garden for the last two hours; it has been almost a bear garden at times, and I was wondering as I sat here just what some of our farmers would think if they could have listened to us for the last two hours. I am making no references to any particular individual, but may I suggest this? So far as I can see, the dispute this afternoon is not so much over the accuracy of the figures that have been presented as with regard to the deductions which have been drawn and the arguments which have been adduced therefrom. It does seem to me that in discussing the varying amounts of butter production during past years we have overlooked what is propably the greatest factor, and that is not the political but the economic factor. I imagine, and I have been in the dairy business for about forty years, that we can divide the dairymen of this country into two classes: first, those to whom dairying is their chief business, those who are professional dairymen, you' might say, who carry on that business year in and year out as their main farming operation, and secondly, those to whom dairying is but a branch of agriculture to be taken up when it seems to be most profitable, and to be dropped when other branches of farming appeal to them as more profitable and as offering perhaps an easier method of making money.
Speaking a year ago on this subject, I made this statement, which I think is absolutely correct and may bear repetition, that the dairy production of this country-and in that I include milk and all its products-might be likened to an index needle which pointed to the condition of the wheat market. During the years when the raising of wheat can be carried on profitably, the second class of dairymen to whom I have referred, to whom dairying is a side issue, will not milk cows;

they will proceed with grain farming. But when prices go down below cost, as they have done of late, they will turn to anything which will bring in a little ready money, and many of them at this time are turning to dairying. It is not a question now of the price of butter or of butter fat. If that were all, they would not be milking cows. But it has come to the point where they are using every possible means in every direction to make a little extra money. At the moment the price of butter fat, I suppose, is lower than it has been since the nineties. A few days ago I received a letter from an outstanding farmer in my district who said that he had always thought I was exaggerating when I told him that in the nineties we sometimes used butter for axle grease, but that now he believed it because they were actually doing it because of the comparatively low price of butter. It does seem to me that we are not gaining very much 'by discussing hour after hour under whose policies this fluctuating production has taken place, because after all it comes down to the economic feature. Men will milk cows when they cannot make money in any other way, or when it seems to them more profit table than any other branch of agriculture. We see that exemplified to-day. The price of butter is very low, the price of butter fat is still lower, but the price of other things,, comparatively, is lower still. That has led to an increased production. Then we had a very open winter last year, one of the most open and most favourable winters for dairy production that we have seen in western Canada for perhaps thirty years. That, coupled with immense quantities of almost valueless feed that was available, has led thousands of men to milk cows during the last few months who had not done so for years. At the present time, therefore, we can look for a continued increase in production. Most certainly we can look to this country being on an export basis for some time to come. That in turn will mean that we must take the export price, which now is moat lamentably low. So far as I can see, the only assistance which can be given to the dairy farmer at the present time by any government, apart from the application of policies which may lower the cost of things which we must buy, reduce the interest on the money which ,the farmer needs to borrow, and lessen the tremendous burdens of indebtedness which the farmer carries, is first, to see that our standards are such that we can compete favourably on the world's market; and second, to see that we suffer no handicap by way of unfair competition from other countries, so

There is a large butter factory in the province of New Brunswick situated within ten miles of one of the best dairying districts in the Dominion of Canada, but the farmers refused to sell their cream to that factory at from 38 to 42 cents. They can make a greater profit by sending their cream to the ice cream manufacturers. I know this to be the fact, because in 1923 when I had the honour of being premier of New Brunswick, the factory at Moncton, which is subsidized to a certain extent by the provincial government, requested the government of that province to guarantee a credit of 850,000 with the Bank of Montreal, to be used as working capital. The reason they asked that guarantee was in order to enable them to hold over the butter they had in storage on August 15, so they might get a better price later in the winter. I looked into the matter, because I wanted to satisfy my-.self that the business was being run properly before arranging for the guarantee of the province, and I discovered that the dairymen of the Salisbury and Petitcodiac districts were refusing to sell their cream to the factory because they were getting a better price from the manufacturers of ice cream. Under those conditions I refused to allow the guarantee of the province to be given; a credit was arranged for, but only to the extent of 835,000. I found later on, when the people could not buy butter, that there were 110,000 pounds in cold storage. The following year I refused the guarantee of the province to anyone who would keep butter in cold storage for that

Mr. Chairman, I am disposed to agree with the last speaker, that we should support the vote. So far as I know the National Dairy Council is not primarily a political organization. Last year I gave some attention to and made some study of the proposal which they made to the tariff advisory board and later to the government, and I thought their request for a four cent duty was a perfectly reasonable one. However, the present government has gone much farther than that and has imposed an eight cent duty. Before I conclude my remarks I intend to ask the Minister of Agriculture to give the committee his frank opinion as to whether he thinks it possible that the imposition of an eight cent duty can do the dairying industry any good for years to come. My opinion is that it is not reasonably possible.
I was much impressed with the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer, and I agree with him when he says that when Canada is on an export basis in regard to butter it is not possible for a protective duty to do the dairying industry any good. It is possible that under a different system of organization some good might be done, if, for instance, the government could control the entire output, as the hon. member for Red Deer says; but so long as there are hundreds of thousands of producers of butter producing and marketing their product on a competitive basis they cannot possibly be benefited by the imposition of a duty because they are bound to take the export price, as is the case at the present time.
I tried ineffectually a few times to get the floor after the hon. member for Stanstead made his somewhat impressive speech. The hon. member presented figures to the committee showing that the Dominion of Canada had between 1925 and 1930 gradually changed from an export to an import basis on butter, and the inference the committee was expected to draw from the figures-the hon. member will correct me if I am wrong-was that the fiscal policy of the preceding administration was the cause of that trend. Our effective competitor during those years was New Zealand and the duty imposed against butter coming from that country was one cent per pound. Although the hon. gentleman did not put it in so many words, he intimated that because of this low duty we had gradually drifted between the years 1925 and 1930 from being on a heavy exporting basis to an im-

porting basis. That is the inference he expected the committee to draw from the figures he placed on Hansard. There never was a more glaring non sequitur. The effective causes which brought this change between 1925 and 1930 were not duties; it was brought about by entirely different factors. The main factor, of course, was the fact that the wheat growers of the west were prospering at wheat growing. As the hon. member for Red Deer pointed out, and as we all know, whatever part of Canada we live in, men prefer to grow wheat to milking cows if they can make as much out of wheat. Certainly they will grow wheat if they are making more at it than they could make by milking cows. So men by the thousands went out of dairying into wheat growing exclusively. That was not attributable to the fiscal policy of any administration, and it was the greatest single factor in preventing a growth in the production of daily products in Canada.
There were other factors as well. There was the great increase in the tourist traffic into this country from the United States. The United States was enjoying a period of piping prosperity. The tourists came across the border in great numbers and -consumed milk products, perhaps largely ice cream, in great quantities. I think I saw somewhere that the tourist consumption of milk and milk products amounted to about 15,000,000 pounds per annum if converted into butter.
In Quebec it was beer.

They may have come for other purposes as well, but the consumption of milk products was incidental to the purposes for which they -came. National Dairy Council of Canada Richmond, P.Q.,
May 18, 1931.
Hon. H. H. Stevens,
Minister of Trade and Commerce,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Stevens:
You asked for a memorandum on the dairy situation with particular reference to the present low price of butter, and the benefit which accrued to the producer from the comparatively high price received for butter before the recent drop.
You will recall that the eight cent tariff against New Zealand made effective October, 1930. had the# effect of raising the price level in this country to about 29 cents, because practically all our purchases of butter were from that dominion. Late in the year the special arrangement with Australia was entered into, whereby they were to sell at not less than 32 cents, pending the ratification of a new trade agreement or at least till the close of the winter or butter import season. Some firming of the world price in London brought New Zealand offerings practically in line with, or slightly above, this artificial price which was maintained within narrow limits till April. The produce trade of this country had offers of butter from Australia for delivery January to April at prices around 22 cents per pound, and this would have been the price level in
this country had the special agreement with Australia not been effected.
Into the nature and merit of this agreement I will not enter for you naturally know more about it than I do, but I merely remind you that it was highly artificial and inelastic, and those connected with the industry soon concluded that this price fixing agreement would be highly effective till it broke down and that then the breakdown would be complete.
We thus had our wholesale butter market maintained all winter at a level from seven to ten cents over world parity, and most of the time at the latter figure. During the period in question about 75,000,000 pounds of butter was produced in this country. We have no accurate statistics of monthly production, but this is a composite of many estimates, and is not far from the truth. All of this production received the full benefit of the artificial price level which thus resulted in an extra return to the producers of about $7,000,000. This, of course, came from the consumers pocket direct, and the consumer in addition paid the extra ten cents on the relatively small amount of Australian butter which entered the country during the period in question.
This figure of $7,000,000 applies to butter only, and does not take account of the fact that prices of whole milk, sweet cream, ice cream, etc., could not have been maintained at the level actually paid if butter had been selling for 22 cents instead of 32 cents. The actual benefit received by dairy producers last winter in the form of extra income was therefore greater than the above figure. I could not hazard a guess at the real total, but am very sure that it was over $10,000,000.
This extra income was invaluable in helping to tide over a critical period for very many farmers, and great credit should be claimed by your government for the action which made this possible.
Let me now discuss the very abrupt fall in the price of butter which took place a few weeks ago, resulting in a fall of 10 cents per pound in as many days, and a later drop which finally took the price down to an extreme low of 19 cents per pound. A number of factors conspired to increase our own make of winter, or fodder butter. Some of these were:-
(a)	The very mild winter in the west.
(b)	The very low price of grain acting both by reducing the cost of raw material, and by forcing farmers to exploit every source of income other than grain selling.
(e) The direct encouragement of a relatively high price, and the assurance of protection.
(d) The diversion of milk and cream formerly shipped to the states, and now shut out by the United States tariff, and by over supply, and low prices across the line.
As a usual thing the supplies of domestic butter coming forward are not much in excess of current consumption till May. It must also be remembered that fodder butter cannot be stored as it is not of good keeping quality, and for similar reasons cannot be exported to advantage. At this time also. New Zealand was selling in London at about 23 cents per pound, which would have meant a price of 20 cents, or less, here for our butter if sold for export. During the month of April the storage stocks at Montreal only declined from 37,702 boxes to 25,933, and most of this decline was

iu the first half of the month This showed that at the end of April the current make was sufficient to take care of the consumption. We had then the following picture:-
(1)	The prospect of a very large summer make.
(2)	The fact that buyers realized that the market was far above world parity, and would have to reach that level before export could take place.
(3)	The receipts mounted rapidly at the last, and were in excess of current requirements.
(4)	No buyer was willing to allow 32 cent butter to accumulate on his hands.
When the break started buyers held off in spite of the, or rather because of the, daily declines till a level was reached at which they had confidence. This was around 19-20 cents at which level export would have been possible, even if not desirable because of the doubtful quality.
The stored stocks which as stated above amounted to nearly 26,000 boxes on May 1st suffered a loss in value of 10 cents per pound, or roughly $150,000.
I have written rather fully in the hope that a clear understanding of all the factors may remove the suspicion which exists in some quarters that the price decline was due to manipulation.
Butter is a perishable commodity, and its market will always be a highly sensitive one. The longer such a market is restrained from moving freely the more violent is the reaction.
The probable increase in production for this year is 15 per cent, or more which would make export possible if not necessary.
If the tariff against Australia (the only one now in doubt) be fixed at a high level there will be great incentive to store butter at present levels, especially if enough be sent out of the country to insure a shortage next winter.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) F. E. M. Robinson, President,
National Dairy Council of Canada.
